headline: Barry identifies a powerful potential coordination between the Fed and Treasury via rolling Fed's maturing Treasury portfolio into the short end rather than pro-rata, avoiding rate impact while addressing debt composition
reasoning: The Fed's Treasury portfolio has an average maturity more than 2.5 years longer than the Treasury market itself, a reversal of the pre-GFC norm. Close to $2 trillion in Fed holdings will mature in coming years; currently these are rolled over pro-rata across the curve. Barry argues the Fed could instead roll maturities into short-end securities, rebalancing its portfolio to pre-crisis norms and giving the Treasury more short-end issuance without increasing supply to the public in a way that moves rates. He frames this as a more powerful and technically cleaner coordination than the buyback program.
quote: The average maturity of what the Fed owns in its Treasury portfolio is more than two and a half years longer than the average maturity in the Treasury market itself. And pre-GFC, what the Fed owned was actually shorter than the Treasury market itself. So there is close to two trillion insecurities from the Fed's portfolio maturing in the next few years. Right now, it rolls them over passively at auction across the curve, pro rata to whatever the Treasury is auctioning, as a passive participant at auction. If it decides to roll them over at the short end instead, it gets the balance sheet back to what it looked like pre-crisis. It also gets the Treasury Department more short-end issuance but not to the public in a way that does not impact rate limits. So I think that's the coordination that's very, very powerful.

headline: Barry argues US fiscal consolidation is the necessary and missing ingredient for any durable reduction in long-end Treasury yields; budget deficits at 6% of GDP during an expansion remain the core constraint
reasoning: Barry notes that fiscal has been absent from the rates conversation for over a year because deficits have been stable, but stable at an historically large 6% of GDP given the position in the economic cycle. He argues that any debt management action — whether buybacks or auction size cuts — cannot durably reduce long-end yields unless accompanied by meaningful fiscal consolidation. He frames the six-month test for whether yesterday's announcement was a turning point as entirely dependent on whether fiscal action follows.
quote: The bigger issue here that we've been grappling with and fiscal hasn't been a part of the conversation for over a year in the U.S. because budget deficits have been stable, but stable at 6% of GDP. So if you're going to take action on this, it needs to be accompanied by some sort of fiscal consolidation. And I think investors with what they've seen here, with rates going back to where they were, are saying we don't see the fiscal consolidation... if we're sitting here six months from now, whether it's been impactful or not is whether it's followed on with any sort of fiscal consolidation to go alongside it.

headline: Barry notes Treasury market liquidity has been at decade-high levels including at the long end, contradicting the stated rationale for the buyback expansion
reasoning: Barry observes that high-level measures of Treasury market liquidity, including dispersion of off-the-runs to the fitted curve (at multi-year lows in both the 10-20y and 20-30y buckets) and liquidity preference metrics, are very close to decade highs. Relative value participants have been complaining about the lack of dislocation opportunities. This directly contradicts the Treasury's stated reasoning of 'strong and consistent offers' warranting larger operations, reinforcing Barry's view that the expansion is politically motivated rather than technically driven.
quote: We've been making the case here, Sam, for like the last six months that Treasury market liquidity has been on a steadily improving trend for the last number of years and in 2026. And when I look in particular at liquidity at the long end of the curve, we talked about dispersion. We talked about liquidity preference. High level measures of liquidity are very close to decade highs. So yes, it's a less liquid point on the curve than the others, but it's been in the context of what has been a steadily improvement in liquidity over the past few years.

headline: Barry warns that elevated T-bill share of outstanding US debt — at recessionary levels during an expansion — limits the Treasury's ability to lean on the bill market in the next downturn
reasoning: Buyback operations fund long-end purchases with new T-bill issuance, increasing the short-end share of outstanding debt. Barry notes T-bill share is already at levels typically seen only during recessions, despite the US being in an economic expansion. He is concerned that the elasticity of demand and inelasticity of pricing that make T-bills attractive in recessions may not be available to the same degree if the starting share is already elevated when the next downturn arrives.
quote: We've heard the argument from investors that the Treasury effectively has unlimited sire power with this program because it's been basically buying back off-the-run securities and funding that with issuance of Treasury bills. They could do this in an unlimited fashion. The theoretically that's true. But we know that the T-bill share of outstanding debt has been on the rise for the last few years. And it is at a relatively high share now, considering we're still in an economic expansion... it's just my fear here that the starting point with the T-bill share at levels that we typically don't see except in recessions, the next time you need to lean on the T-bill market for an increase in issuance the next recession, you may not have the same benefits you had in the past.

headline: J.P. Morgan rates strategist Jay Barry sees Treasury's surprise buyback expansion as a signal of administration discomfort with rising long-end yields rather than a genuine liquidity need
reasoning: Barry argues that none of the three TBAC-derived metrics that justify scaling up buybacks — offer-to-max ratios, dispersion along a fitted curve, or off-the-run discount to on-the-runs — actually warrant the change. He links it to other interventions (EUR/JPY FX intervention, changed refunding guidance) as a coordinated effort to stem the rise in long-term rates.
quote: So the read-through for me, this announcement yesterday, alongside the very curious change that the Treasury Department made to its guidance that the obvious refunding two weeks ago, as well as the intervention that was done in Euro-EN, all reads that they're attempting to sort of stem the tide here in long-term rates, perhaps until they see more decisive action on the monetary normalization side from the Bank of Japan. So I think it all comes down to discomfort with rate levels, knowing that the Fed is not, I wouldn't say being uncooperative, but sees no reason to cut rates. And other factors globally are pointing to higher rates as well. So I think it's an effort to make good on this, knowing that we have the midterm elections in two and a half months.

headline: Barry identifies Japan as a key driver of US long-end yield pressure, worth roughly 20bp, as the BoJ's yield curve normalization exports higher rates globally

Now the opposite is true — when global yields move higher, particularly in Japan, it exerts upward pressure on US long-end rates. He estimates the Japan effect is worth around 20bp and suggests the appropriate response is more aggressive BoJ monetary action rather than US debt management maneuvers.
quote: I think there is growing discomfort with the level of yields. We know this administration and this Treasury Secretary have had a desire to lower interest rates... on the layer on top of that at the long end of the curve, I think there's also a read-through that global capital flows matter... when global yields move higher, it's got an impact to move the U.S. And we know that the long end of the end curve has been moving significantly this year... Japan is a key factor there. It's worth maybe 20 basis points though. So yes, it's worth something. But you as the debt manager of the largest government bond market in the world, like is something like 20 basis points that should be focused on when it's kind of exogenous to what's happening and probably requires more aggressive monetary action from Japan to take that on.

And on top of that we had work on this done in a charge in a last quarterly refunding announcement that we got in May and the presenter of that charge question on this topic noted that the economic value is different in different reserve regimes. So it's positive when reserves are scarce, modestly positive and reserves are ample and negative in abundant reserve environments. reasoning: The Asia-Europe LNG arbitrage has remained open in favour of Asia since the start of the Middle East conflict, with Asian spot prices reaching nearly $4/MMBTU premium at the outset and still trading at ~$1.3-$1.4/MMBTU premium. This is diverting marginal spot cargoes to Asia rather than Europe. Northwest European storage is running at roughly 50%, the lowest historically, versus ~55% last year (which was itself a record low). The gap has widened from 7 percentage points at end of March to approximately 15 percentage points currently, and continues to widen.
quote: The Asia-Europe ARB, if you will, it's been pretty consistent from the beginning of the conflict and it's been open in favor of Asia. The premiums of Asian spot prices reached almost $4 per MMBTU at the beginning of the conflict. It stayed at around $2 per MMBTU throughout the quarter and it's still trading about $1.3, $1.4 premium, which means that for marginal spot cargos, Asia remains the more preferable option to deliver these cargos. This obviously having an impact on European situation where the storages are running at historical lows in northwest Europe at around 50% compared to around 55% this time last year, which was the lowest. More importantly, this gap keeps widening. So 40 versus 55, we have about 15% gap at the moment. This was only 7% as of end of March.

headline: J.P. Morgan concedes its original oil price framework was directionally right on the supply shock but wrong on the clearing mechanism and resulting price level
reasoning: J.P. Morgan's original Brent price forecast assumed the Strait of Hormuz would reopen June 1, prices would average ~$100/bbl from March to June, and the physical market would adjust roughly equally through demand losses and inventory draws, with the bulk of adjustment coming from strategic reserves. The market largely followed the first part — prices spiked — but the composition of the market clearing mechanism differed substantially: demand losses were far larger and commercial inventory draws far smaller than modelled. The physical market is actually tighter than the original model implied (given delayed upstream restart), yet prices are lower, which the team attributes entirely to the demand-destruction clearing channel suppressing price signals. This is acknowledged as a significant analytical miss requiring a full framework reassessment.
quote: So this conclusion forced us to look elsewhere. So adjustments in the physical commodity markets that we have discussed in previous podcasts can occur through three separate channels... While the overall magnitude of the rebalancing appears broadly consistent with our expectations, the composition has been materially different. For example, strategic petroleum reserves releases appear to have occurred largely in Wang Bizao original assumptions, yet the key divergence instead came from two other variables, OECD commercial inventories decline materially less than expected, while demand losses during March and April appear to have been substantially larger. This distinction matters enormously for the price formation.
